lesson.title: Strategic choices

lead.text: Before the phone networks, a smaller case where the numbers are easy to follow. Two cafés, Ruby's and Sol's, face each other across one street. Each owner decides every evening whether to close early or stay open late. Each choice is called a strategy, and what a café earns depends on both owners' strategies together.

A table keeps track of this. The rows are Ruby's strategies and the columns are Sol's. Each cell holds a pair of numbers, Ruby's profit first and Sol's second, in thousands of pounds a week. Such a table is called a payoff matrix, and a payoff is what a player earns from an outcome.

afterFigure.text: Read the top-left cell first. If both cafés close early, each makes £8k. In the bottom-left cell Ruby stays open late while Sol closes early, so Ruby takes the late trade: £12k for her and only £3k for him. In the bottom-right cell both stay open late. They split the late trade and each pays for staff and lighting, so each makes £6k. The second case is a quieter street, with the same shape and smaller numbers.

steps.headline: The best reply to a choice

lead.text: Now sit in Ruby's seat. She does not know what Sol will do, but she can ask a smaller question: for each thing Sol might do, which of her two strategies pays more? Answering for one choice at a time is easy, because only one column of the table matters.

Suppose Sol closes early. In that column Ruby earns £8k by closing early too and £12k by staying open, so staying open is better. Suppose instead Sol stays open late. Now Ruby earns £3k by closing early and £6k by staying open, so staying open is better again. The strategy that pays a player most against a given choice by the rival is called her best response to it.
Finding a best response always works the same way. Hold the rival's choice fixed, then compare your own payoffs. The next question gives you that job in a different table.
Two phone networks, Alpha and Beta, each set a High or a Low monthly price. Hold one of Beta's choices fixed and compare Alpha's payoffs against it.

steps.headline: A strategy that wins either way

lead.text: Ruby's answer was the same both times. Staying open late was her best response when Sol closed early and her best response when Sol stayed open. A strategy that is the best response to every choice the rival might make is called a dominant strategy. Its advantage is that a player does not have to guess what the rival will do, because the same strategy is best either way.
Sol's payoffs mirror Ruby's, so staying open late is dominant for him too. The figure marks the best responses in each column and row.

afterFigure.text: Not every game gives a player a dominant strategy. If one strategy wins against one choice and loses against another, the player has to guess. Here both owners have one, so neither needs to guess and both stay open late, earning £6k each. That is less than the £8k each would earn if both closed early, and a later screen returns to that.

lead.text: Back to the phone networks. Alpha's payoffs are in the matrix. Find which price pays Alpha more against each of Beta's choices, and decide whether one price wins both times.

reveal.text: You tested Alpha's best response against both of Beta's choices. When one strategy wins both times it is dominant, and Alpha needs no forecast of Beta.

lead.text: Both cafés have a dominant strategy, so we can say where they end up: both open late. Look at that bottom-right cell from the inside. If Ruby alone closed early she would drop from £6k to £3k, and if Sol alone closed early he would drop the same way. Neither gains by changing their own choice while the other holds still, so neither moves.

An outcome with that property is called a Nash equilibrium, after the mathematician John Nash. In it each player's strategy is a best response to the other's. The test is the one you have been using: take a cell and let each player switch alone in turn. If neither gains, the cell is an equilibrium.

afterFigure.text: Some games have more than one equilibrium. Take two drivers who meet on a narrow road, each choosing to keep left or keep right. If both keep left, or both keep right, they pass safely. If they choose different sides they collide. Both-left and both-right are each stable, because a driver who switches alone causes a crash. A mismatch is not stable, because a driver in it gains by switching to the other's side.

steps.headline: Price war: Alpha and Beta each choose High or Low. Find the Nash equilibrium.

workedSteps.text: Find Alpha's best response to each of Beta's choices.
workedSteps.math: Against High: Low pays 14, High pays 10. Against Low: Low pays 5, High pays 2.

workedSteps.text: Beta's payoffs mirror Alpha's, so Low is Beta's best response as well.
Both play Low, and each earns 5.

steps.headline: Two makers each choose plug standard A or B. Matching on A pays 6 each; matching on B pays 4 each; a mismatch pays nothing. Find the Nash equilibria.

workedSteps.text: At A/A, suppose Maker A switches alone to B while Maker B stays on A.
That is below the 6 A earned, so A/A is an equilibrium. B/B works the same way: a lone switch drops a maker from 4 to nothing.
A mismatched cell is not an equilibrium: a maker there earns nothing and gains by switching.
Count the cells where neither maker gains by switching alone.

lead.text: Look again at the cafés' equilibrium. Both stay open late and each earns £6k. If both had closed early, each would have earned £8k, so both would be better off. Yet neither will close early, because whichever way the other goes, closing early alone pays less. The equilibrium is stable, and it is worse for both players than another outcome they could have reached.

A game with this shape is called a prisoner's dilemma. The name comes from the story of two suspects held in separate rooms. Each is better off confessing whatever the other does, yet if both confess they do worse than if both stayed silent.

Rival firms can fall into the same trap. They could agree to keep prices high, but each would be tempted to undercut, and a firm that keeps to the agreement while the other undercuts loses most. The next question looks at the price war between the phone networks, where that happens.
Back in the price war, both firms play their dominant strategy. Look up what each earns there and add the two together.

reveal.text: Both choose Low and earn £5m each, £10m together, though High/High would give £20m. Each firm's best choice leaves both worse off: a prisoner's dilemma.

lead.text: So far the cafés and the networks met once. Most rivals meet again, and that changes what a choice means. Staying open late undercuts Sol today, but he can remember it. A game played over several rounds by the same players is called a repeated game.

In a repeated game a player can react to what the rival did before. One simple rule is tit for tat: be friendly in the first round, then copy whatever the rival did in the round before. Against a friendly rival it stays friendly. Against one who undercuts, it undercuts back from the next round on.

afterFigure.text: Take three rounds. If Ruby plays tit for tat and Sol always stays open late, round one costs Ruby: she closes early for £3k while Sol takes £12k. After that she copies him, so rounds two and three are open against open at £6k each. Her total is 3 + 6 + 6 = £15k, against £18k if she had stayed open all three rounds. If both play tit for tat, both close early every round and each earns 3 × £8k = £24k. The threat of being copied is what makes the friendly choice pay, so repetition can make cooperation worthwhile.

cases.label: Ruby tit for tat v Sol always open late

lead.text: Now the phone networks meet for five rounds. Alpha plays tit for tat: High first, then it copies Beta's last move. Beta always sets Low.

reveal.text: Alpha is undercut once, then matches Low: £22m, while Beta earns £34m. Against another tit-for-tat player Alpha would earn £10m a round. When a game repeats, the threat of retaliation can make cooperation pay.

lesson.orientation: Find best responses, dominant strategies and Nash equilibria in payoff matrices, and see how repetition supports cooperation.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: The ferry owner in the last lesson had to think about her buyers and nobody else. Her price was hers to choose and no rival could answer it. Most firms are not so lucky. A phone network or an airline on a busy route shares its market with a few rivals, and what any one of them earns depends on what the others do.

Take two networks, Alpha and Beta, that serve one town. Each is about to set a monthly price, High or Low. If both charge High, both do well. If Alpha charges Low while Beta stays High, Alpha takes customers from Beta and does better still, while Beta's profit falls. Beta has the same thought about Alpha, and each knows the other is thinking it.

So neither can settle on a price alone. This lesson gives a way to reason about that. It starts with a table of every combination of choices, uses the table to find what each firm should do, and ends with what changes when the same firms meet again.

intro.promise: By the end you'll predict what two rival firms will choose, and say why meeting repeatedly can make cooperation pay.

recap.keyIdea: Your best choice depends on the other player's. A Nash equilibrium is where nobody gains by switching alone, and it can leave everyone worse off, as in a prisoner's dilemma. Repetition can make cooperation pay, because a rival can punish.

blocks.text: You found Low dominant for both networks, so they earned £10m between them instead of £20m. A tit-for-tat Alpha still took £22m over five rounds against a rival who always cut.

recap.nextHook: That is the last lesson of the course. The tools work best together, so pick a market you know and ask who sets its price, and what each seller would do if a rival moved first.

questions.prompt: Alpha and Beta each set a High or a Low price. If Beta sets High, Alpha earns £10m with High and £14m with Low. If Beta sets Low, Alpha earns £2m with High and £5m with Low. Which price is a dominant strategy for Alpha? Answer High or Low.
hints: Find Alpha's best response to each of Beta's choices.
A dominant strategy is the best response to every choice the rival makes.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Low: it pays Alpha more whatever Beta does.

questions.onCorrect: Low. It pays more against High (£14m to £10m) and against Low (£5m to £2m).

questions.prompt: In the price war between Alpha and Beta, Low is each firm's dominant strategy, so both set Low. What combined profit, in £m, do the two firms earn there?
hints: Find the cell where both firms set Low.
Read both payoffs in that cell.
Add them.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Low/Low gives £5m + £5m = £10m, half the £20m of High/High.

questions.onCorrect: £10m. Both play Low, earning £5m each, half of the £20m that High/High would give.

misconceptions.feedback: That is each firm's profit. The question asks for the combined profit.

questions.prompt: Alpha and Beta play their price game for five rounds. Alpha plays tit for tat (High in round one, then it copies Beta's last move) and Beta always sets Low. A lone High pays £2m, a lone Low pays £14m and Low/Low pays £5m each. What is Alpha's total profit over the five rounds, in £m?

In round one only Alpha sets High.
Add Alpha's payoff across all five rounds.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Round one: Alpha High, Beta Low, so Alpha earns £2m. Rounds two to five: Low/Low, £5m each. Total 2 + 4 × 5 = £22m.

questions.onCorrect: £22m. One undercut costs Alpha once; after that it matches Low and loses little more.

misconceptions.feedback: That is Beta's total. Alpha earns less.
